Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

For $n\ge1$, let $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the $R$-coefficients of [[def-bruhat-interval-and-r-polynomials]]. (a) **Recursion.** Let $w\in S_n$ and let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection with $sw<w$. Then for every $y\in S_n$ $$r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}\quad\text{if }sy<y,\qquad r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}+(v-v^{-1})\,r_{y,sw}\quad\text{if }sy>y .$$ (b) **Support.** $r_{y,w}\ne0$ implies $y\le w$, and $r_{w,w}=1$. (c) **Degree and parity.** For $y\le w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $r_{y,w}\in v^{-d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{2},v^{-2}]$; the term of least $v$-degree is $\mathrm{sgn}(y)\,\mathrm{sgn}(w)\,v^{-d}$, and the term of largest $v$-degree is $v^{d}$. (d) **Symmetry.** $\overline{r_{y,w}}=\mathrm{sgn}(y)\mathrm{sgn}(w)r_{y,w}$ and $r_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=r_{y,w}$. (e) **Matrix inversion.** $\sum_{y\in S_n} r_{x,y}\,\overline{r_{y,z}}=\delta_{x,z}$ for all $x,z$; equivalently the triangular matrices $R=(r_{x,y})$, $\bar R$ satisfy $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$. Here $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$ and all coefficients are kept in the variable $v$ of this page.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

derivations.claim: **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2).

**The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$.

**The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below.

**The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$.

**Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4).

**The generator trace identity.** By step 6.1, for every $w$ and simple reflection $s$ one has $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\delta_{w,s^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_sH_w)=\delta_{s,w^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$. Extending over the standard basis gives $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$. In particular the common value for $w=s$ is $1$.

**$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$.

**Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. A nonzero term requires $u\le x$ and $u\le y$; if $x
e y$, every surviving term has a factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, because $u<x$ or $u<y$ is [F3], and $u=x
e y$ gives $h_{x,y}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ when $x<y$ and $h_{x,y}=0$ otherwise, symmetrically for $u=y$; hence $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $x
e y$. For $x=y$ the term $u=x$ contributes $h_{x,x}^2=1$ and every other term has $u<x$ and contributes to $v^2\mathbb Z[v]$, so $(\underline H_x,\underline H_x)\in 1+v\mathbb Z[v]$.

**The standard pairing (6) and conclusion.** By (4) the form $(-,-)$ is the $A$-bilinear form whose matrix in the normalized standard basis $\{H_x\}$ is the identity; the published type-A Soergel Hom formula uses the standard pairing with $\langle H_x,H_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$ on that normalized basis, and the dictionary of [F4] fixes the normalization $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and the resulting Kazhdan-Lusztig coefficients, so the transported pairing agrees with $(-,-)$ on the basis and hence on $H$ by bilinearity. All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice.

citations.quote: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that by
[[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] the
multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ and the characters
$h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(M)$ are defined and intrinsic. Then for every simple
reflection $s=s_i$:

1. $B_i\otimes_RM$ and $M\otimes_RB_i$ lie in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, with
   finitely many flag quotients;
2. $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$, where
   $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_i+v$ and $\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ is the
   normalized basis of [[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]];
3. for the internal shift and all $k\in\mathbb Z$,
   $h_\Delta(M\{k\})=v^{-k}h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(M\{k\})=v^{k}h_\nabla(M)$; in the Elias–Williamson notation of the
   sources, whose shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ lowers every generating degree by one,
   this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$ and $h_\nabla$ by
   $v^{-1}$;
4. on $M=R$ the recursion reads $h_\Delta(B_i)=h_\nabla(B_i)=H_i$.

This is a statement about the action of the generators only: multiplicativity of
$h_\Delta$ and $h_\nabla$ for arbitrary tensor products is proved on this page
only after the categorification theorem.

Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. **The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.

Let $\underline x$ be a reduced expression for $x\in S_n$ and let $F_{\underline x}$ be the Rouquier complex $F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$ (or its minimal subcomplex). Then for every $y\in S_n$ there is an isomorphism in the homotopy category of graded bimodules
$$\Gamma_{\ge y}(F_{\underline x})/\Gamma_{>y}(F_{\underline x})\;\cong\;\begin{cases}\Delta_x,&y=x,\\0,&y\ne x,\end{cases}$$
where $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. Equivalently: the Bruhat support subquotient of a positive Rouquier complex is contractible except in the top layer $\Delta_x$; $F_{\underline x}$ is $\Delta$-split in the sense that each of its support subquotients is a direct sum of standard bimodules, and the top layer is a single $\Delta_x$. No positivity of characters and no assumption $\mathrm{S}$ is used; the statement is unconditional for every finite type-$A$ Coxeter group and the coordinate reflection realization.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

derivations.claim: **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the Rouquier complex is the unit $S$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$, so $^0F_e=S=B_e$, there is no term of index $i\ge1$, both perverse bounds hold trivially, and the only nonzero inverse coefficient is $g_{e,e}=1$; for $x=s_i$ the complex $F_{s_i}=[B_{s_i}^R\to S(1)]$ has $^0F_{s_i}=B_{s_i}$ and $^1F_{s_i}=S(1)=B_e^R(1)$ and no other term, so $m_{e,1}=1$ with $\ell(s_i)-\ell(e)=1\equiv1\pmod2$, $B_{s_i}$ is perverse by $\mathrm S(s_i)$ and $S(1)$ is the shift of the perverse unit, so $F_{s_i}\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$ and $g_{s_i,s_i}=1$, $g_{e,s_i}=-v$.

**Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$, write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ with $m\ge1$ and put $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$, $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$; the hypothesis $\mathrm S(\le x)$ contains $\mathrm S(\le y)$, and we assume the three assertions of the statement for $y$: $^0F_y=B_y$, $^iF_y=\bigoplus_{z<y}B_z(i)^{m^y_{z,i}}$ for $i\ge1$, and $F_y\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$. By [F1], $F_x\cong F_yF_s$ in $K^b$.

**Descent contraction.** Let $z$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs<z$ and $\mathrm S(z)$; then $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$ in $K^b$. Indeed, by [F2] the two-term complex $B_zF_s$ has terms $B_zB_s=B_z(1)\oplus B_z(-1)$ in degree $0$ and $B_z(1)$ in degree $1$, with differential $d=(\delta,\eta)$ where $\delta\in\operatorname{End}^0(B_z(1))=\operatorname{End}^0(B_z)=\mathbb R$ by [F2] and [F6]. If $\delta=0$ then $B_zF_s$ is the direct sum of the two nonzero complexes $[B_z(1)\to0]$ and $[B_z(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta\ }B_z(1)]$, contradicting the indecomposability of $B_zF_s$, which is the image of the indecomposable $B_z$ under the equivalence $-\otimes F_s$; hence $\delta\ne0$ is an isomorphism, homological Gaussian elimination cancels the contractible two-term complex $B_z(1)\cong B_z(1)$, and the remainder is $B_z(-1)$ concentrated in degree $0$.

**Top support and the Euler character.** Every positive-degree term of the word complex omits at least one letter, so no such term has the $x$ graph by [F3]. The degree-zero term is its reduced word, whose top summand is exactly $B_x$ unshifted and once. Gaussian minimalization cannot remove it, since no target term has its label. Thus in the minimal complex $m^0_{x,0}=1$ and every other $m^i_{x,k}$ is zero, by actual support rather than alternating cancellation. Character additivity makes its Euler character unchanged by removing a contractible pair. The generator recursion and shift rule in [F3] give $\operatorname{ch}(F_zF_s)=\operatorname{ch}(F_z)(\underline H_s-v)$ degree by degree. Iterating along the reduced word therefore gives Euler character $H_x$. Under the stated $S(\le x)$, expanding each actual summand character in the KL basis yields $\sum_{i,k}(-1)^im^i_{w,k}v^k=g_{w,x}$. This equality is used only for the Euler coefficients, after the support proof of the top multiplicity.

**Ascent perverse bound.** Let $z\le y$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs>z$; then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$. Indeed, $\mathrm S(u)$ holds for every $u<zs$, because $u<zs\le x$ implies $u<x$; so [F2] gives the unshifted decomposition $B_zB_s=B_{zs}\oplus\bigoplus_{u<zs}B_u^{a_u}$, whose summands are perverse by $\mathrm S(zs)$ and $\mathrm S(u)$, while the second term $B_z(1)$ of $B_zF_s=[B_zB_s\to B_z(1)]$ is the internal shift of the perverse $B_z$ sitting in cohomological degree $1$; thus the chosen representative has p-split terms and satisfies $\tau_{<0}(B_zB_s)=0$ and $\tau_{<-1}(B_z(1))=0$, which is membership in $pK^b_{\ge0}$ by [F5].

**Shift propagation.** Assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$ and let $F_x$ be minimal. If $^iF_x$ contains a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then $^{i-1}F_x$ contains a summand $B_{z'}(j')$ with $z'>z$ and $j'<j$. First, components of the differential into summands of shift $k<j$ vanish: a degree-zero map $B_z(j)\to B_u(k)$ is an element of $\operatorname{Hom}^{k-j}(B_z,B_u)$, which is zero for $k<j$ since the graded Hom space has no negative-degree part by [F6]; components with $k=j$ are zero for $u\ne z$ by [F6] and are scalars for $u=z$, and a nonzero scalar component would make $B_z(j)$ a contractible summand of the minimal complex, so all such components vanish as well; hence $d(B_z(j))$ lies in the sum of the summands of $^{i+1}F_x$ with shift $k>j$. Second, if a summand $B_u(k)$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ maps nontrivially to $B_z(j)$, then $k<j$: a degree-zero map $B_u(k)\to B_z(j)$ lies in $\operatorname{Hom}^{j-k}(B_u,B_z)$, which vanishes for $j<k$, and for $j=k$ it vanishes for $u\ne z$ and is a scalar for $u=z$, the nonzero case again being excluded by minimality. Third, apply the support cutoff $\Gamma_{\ge z/>z}$ and reduce its free graph modules modulo $R_+$. Since $z<x$, its complex is contractible by [F5], hence this reduced finite-dimensional complex is exact. The chosen top layer $\Delta_z(j)$ of $B_z(j)$ is a nonzero homogeneous basis vector. Every outgoing target has shift $k>j$, and its $z$ layer has shift $k+d$ with $d\ge0$ by KL triangularity. A map from the chosen generator into it consequently has positive-degree coefficient, so vanishes after reduction. The chosen vector is a cycle and must therefore be an incoming boundary. Some incoming component has a nonzero constant coefficient onto it, so some $B_{z'}(j')$ in degree $i-1$ has a $z$ layer with $j'+d=j$. The underlying differential component is nonzero, and the preceding Hom estimate gives $j'<j$. Since $d=0$ for label $z$ itself, this requires $z'>z$. This proves shift propagation without using an Euler identity to recover multiplicities.

**The perverse lower bound for $F_x$.** Use the stupid filtration $w_{\ge k}F_y$ of the minimal complex $F_y$, with distinguished triangles $w_{\ge k+1}F_y\to w_{\ge k}F_y\to{}^kF_y[-k]\to$ and $w_{\ge\ell(y)+1}F_y=0$; tensoring with the invertible $F_s$ preserves distinguished triangles. We prove $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by descending induction on $k$: for $k=\ell(y)+1$ the object is $0$; assume it for $k+1$. By [ih] and step 2.1, $^kF_y$ is a direct sum of summands $B_z(k)$ with $z\le y$ (with $z=y$ only for $k=0$), so $(^kF_y)F_s[-k]$ is a direct sum of copies of $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]$. If $zs>z$ then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by step 4.1, and its internal shift $(k)$ and homological shift $[-k]$ place every summand $B_u(\ell)$ occurring in cohomological degree $i$ into degree $i+k$ with internal shift $\ell+k\le i+k$, so $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; if $zs<z$  then step 3.1 gives $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$, so $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]\cong B_z(k-1)[-k]$, a perverse object with internal shift $k-1$ in cohomological degree $k$, again in $pK^b_{\ge0}$. Extension closure of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ in the tensored triangles gives $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$, and at $k=0$ we obtain $F_yF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; by step 2.1 this is $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$.

**The top term and the perverse upper bound.** If $^0F_x$ contained a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then step 4.2 with $i=0$ would produce a summand of $^{-1}F_x=0$, which is impossible; hence every summand of $^0F_x$ has label $x$, and by step 3.2 ($m^0_{x,0}=1$ and $m^0_{x,k}=0$ for $k\ne0$) we get $^0F_x=B_x$, which proves (1). Now suppose $i\ge1$ and $^iF_x$ has a summand $B_z(k)$ with $k<i$; if $z=x$ this contradicts $m^i_{x,k}=0$ from step 3.2, so $z<x$, and step 4.2 produces a summand $B_{z'}(k')$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ with $k'<k<i$. This summand is again of the forbidden type: if $z'=x$ then $m^{i-1}_{x,k'}=0$ whenever $i-1\ge1$, while for $i-1=0$ it contradicts $^0F_x=B_x$ because $k'<0$; otherwise $z'<x$ and step 4.2 applies again. Iterating this descent in the homological degree we reach a summand of $^0F_x$ with negative internal shift, contradicting $^0F_x=B_x$. Hence every summand of $^iF_x$ has internal shift $\ge i$ for $i\ge1$, which together with $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ from step 5.1 gives $F_x\in pK^b_{\le0}$; since for $i\ge1$ the label $x$ does not occur by step 3.2, we obtain $^iF_x=\bigoplus_{z<x}B_z(i)^{m_{z,i}}$ with $m_{z,i}:=m^i_{z,i}$, which is (2).

**Inversion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig transition matrix.** Let the two bases be related by $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}h_{y,w}H_y$ and $H_w=\sum_{y\le w}g_{y,w}\underline H_y$ as in [F4]; substituting the first expansion into the second gives $\sum_{y\le z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}=\delta_{y,w}$. Hence $g_{w,w}=1$ and, for $y<w$, $g_{y,w}=-\sum_{y<z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}$. We prove $g_{y,w}\in v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by descending induction on $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: for $y=w$ this is $1\in v^0\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$, and for $y<w$ each $h_{y,z}$ lies in $v^{\ell(z)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by [F4] and each $g_{z,w}$ with $y<z\le w$ lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by the hypothesis of the induction, so each product lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ and the finite sum does too.

**Parity and positivity of the inverse coefficients.** By step 3.2 and step 6.1 the multiplicities appearing in $g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^im_{z,i}v^i$ are exactly the multiplicities of the linear complex $F_x$, and by step 7.1 we have $g_{z,x}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; therefore the coefficient $(-1)^im_{z,i}$ of $v^i$ can be nonzero only when $i\equiv\ell(x)-\ell(z)\pmod2$, which is the parity clause of (3). For such $i$ the sign $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}$ equals $+1$, so $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}m_{z,i}v^i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v^{\pm1}]$, and the coefficients are the nonnegative multiplicities $m_{z,i}$. This proves (3) and, with (1) and (2), completes the induction.

boundaries.evidence: The empty word is the base of the induction and is discharged at the start of step 1.1: the complex is the unit in degree zero, there are no higher terms, both perverse bounds are trivial and the multiplicity statement is vacuous.

The degree-zero term is pinned down in step 6.1: a lower summand there would propagate to a summand of the term in degree -1, which is zero, so the top term is exactly the indecomposable; the vanishing of the negative terms is what drives the argument.

The unit-length word is the first nontrivial instance of the induction: step 2.1 sets up the last letter with the induction hypothesis for the shorter word, and step 3.1 handles the descent contraction used when that letter lowers the length.

Non-reduced or non-minimal representatives are excluded by the hypotheses rather than assumed away: step 5.1 splits off the contractible summand of the perverse truncation and step 3.1 performs the descent contraction only across an invertible differential block.

The two perverse bounds are the grading endpoints: step 4.1 proves the lower bound for the ascent complex, step 6.1 the upper bound, and linearity pins each summand of the degree-indexed term at exactly the matching internal shift.
Choice-free: the induction runs over the finite set of permutations, and every cancellation in steps 3.1 and 5.1 is performed on an explicitly invertible block.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a list of structural conclusions about a minimal complex; it states no equivalence, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse is claimed: the linearity and multiplicity statements are proved directly from the character hypotheses, not as one side of a biconditional.
